front: Which communications technology carries most international internet data between continents?
back: Undersea fibre-optic cables
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How have communications systems such as the internet and mobile phones driven globalisation?
back: They allow instant, cheap contact and control of operations worldwide
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How did deregulation of financial markets act as a factor in globalisation?
back: Capital could move freely and quickly between countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How does electronic, 24-hour trading on stock exchanges help globalisation?
back: Money moves instantly between financial centres in different time zones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How do security systems, such as encrypted online payments, act as a factor in globalisation?
back: They make e-commerce and international payments safe, so trade grows
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How do information systems such as barcodes and tracking help globalisation?
back: TNCs track goods along global supply chains in real time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: How do trade agreements act as a factor in globalisation?
back: They cut tariffs and quotas, so trade between members grows
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a tariff?
back: A tax on imported goods
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a quota in international trade?
back: A limit on the amount of a good that can be imported
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is the term for a barrier to trade that is not a tax, such as strict product standards?
back: A non-tariff barrier
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is free trade?
back: Trade between countries with no tariffs, quotas or other barriers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is protectionism?
back: Using tariffs, quotas or subsidies to shield home industries from imports
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Which political and economic approach of the 1980s favoured free markets, privatisation and deregulation?
back: Neoliberalism
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Give an example of political globalisation.
back: Countries joining international organisations and treaties, such as the UN
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: Give an example of social globalisation.
back: Spread of ideas and culture through migration, tourism and the internet
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.1 Globalisation

front: What is a global system?
back: A set of interconnected parts (states, firms, flows) working at a global scale
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is interdependence?
back: When countries rely on each other, so a change in one affects others
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is economic interdependence?
back: Countries relying on each other for trade, investment, jobs and supply chains
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is political interdependence?
back: Countries linked through alliances, treaties and international organisations
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is social interdependence?
back: Links between people in different countries through migration, culture and family ties
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is environmental interdependence?
back: Environmental change in one place has consequences for environments elsewhere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Why are all countries environmentally interdependent?
back: They share global commons such as the atmosphere and oceans
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can flows of FDI promote growth in a host country?
back: They bring jobs, skills, technology and tax revenue
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can flows of remittances promote development?
back: Families spend them on food, housing, education and healthcare
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can unequal flows of money cause inequality within a country?
back: Investment concentrates in a few cities or regions, widening the gap with rural areas
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In global systems, what is an injustice?
back: Unfair treatment of people or places, such as exploitative pay and conditions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can global demand for resources cause conflict?
back: Groups or states fight over control of valuable resources such as oil or minerals
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Which sociologist developed world systems theory (1974)?
back: Immanuel Wallerstein
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, which three zones make up the world economy?
back: Core, semi-periphery and periphery
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, what is the core?
back: Rich states with high-skill, high-wage, high-tech production that dominate the system
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, what is the periphery?
back: Poor states supplying raw materials and cheap labour to the core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: In Wallerstein's world systems theory, what is the semi-periphery?
back: States with features of both core and periphery, such as emerging economies
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: According to Wallerstein, how does the core benefit from the periphery?
back: Unequal exchange transfers wealth from periphery to core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Who argued in 1967 that rich countries cause the 'development of underdevelopment' in poor countries?
back: Andre Gunder Frank (dependency theory)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What does dependency theory argue?
back: Poor countries stay poor because they depend on and are exploited by rich ones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is neo-colonialism?
back: Control of poorer countries by richer states or TNCs through economic power, not direct rule
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is hegemony?
back: Dominance of one state over others through economic, military or cultural power
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is a superpower?
back: A state able to project its power and influence anywhere in the world
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is geopolitics?
back: How geography, power and politics combine to shape relations between states
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Who coined the term 'soft power'?
back: Joseph Nye
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is soft power?
back: Influence through attraction, such as culture and values, rather than force
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is hard power?
back: Influence through military force or economic pressure, such as sanctions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How do powerful states drive global systems to their own advantage?
back: They set rules in bodies like the IMF, WTO and UN Security Council
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: How can smaller, weaker states resist powerful states in global systems?
back: By forming blocs or alliances to bargain together
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Why are countries that depend on one primary export vulnerable?
back: A fall in its world price cuts export earnings sharply
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What do terms of trade measure?
back: The price of a country's exports relative to the price of its imports
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What does the Prebisch-Singer hypothesis argue about primary product exporters?
back: Their terms of trade tend to worsen over time against manufactured goods
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: What is the digital divide?
back: The gap between people with and without access to the internet and digital technology
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Why can a financial crisis in one country spread worldwide?
back: Banks and markets are interdependent, so losses pass between them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.2 Global systems

front: Since 1950, how has the growth of world trade compared with the growth of world output (GDP)?
back: Trade has grown faster than output
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How has the share of world trade between developing countries (south-south trade) changed in recent decades?
back: It has grown rapidly
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is intra-firm trade?
back: Trade between branches of the same TNC in different countries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a trading bloc?
back: A group of countries that agree to reduce or remove trade barriers between members
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a free trade area?
back: Members remove tariffs between themselves but keep their own tariffs on others
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does a customs union add to a free trade area?
back: A common external tariff on imports from non-members
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does a common (single) market add to a customs union?
back: Free movement of labour, capital and services
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a bilateral trade agreement?
back: A trade deal between two countries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a multilateral trade agreement?
back: A trade deal among many countries, such as through the WTO
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is trade diversion?
back: Trade shifting from a cheaper outside supplier to a member of the same bloc
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a trade surplus?
back: When the value of a country's exports is greater than its imports
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a trade deficit?
back: When the value of a country's imports is greater than its exports
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the term for higher tariffs on processed goods than on raw materials?
back: Tariff escalation
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How does tariff escalation harm developing countries?
back: It discourages them from processing raw materials and adding value
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is added value?
back: The increase in worth of a product at each stage of processing
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How do farm subsidies in rich countries harm farmers in poorer countries?
back: Subsidised crops are sold cheaply on world markets, undercutting them
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is dumping in international trade?
back: Selling exports abroad below the cost of production
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is preferential access in trade?
back: Lower or no tariffs for goods from particular countries, often the poorest
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the WTO term for special rights that give developing countries more time and better market access?
back: Special and Differential Treatment
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How can differential access to markets reduce a country's economic well-being?
back: Exports face high barriers, so jobs and income from trade are lost
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How can access to a large market improve a country's societal well-being?
back: Trade income funds better health and education services
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why do landlocked countries often have weaker access to world markets?
back: They pay more to move goods through other countries to ports
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why can membership of a trade bloc be a risk for a smaller economy?
back: It becomes dependent on bigger members, so their recessions hit it hard
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does Fairtrade guarantee producers?
back: A minimum price plus a social premium for community projects
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a transnational corporation (TNC)?
back: A company that operates in more than one country
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Where are a TNC's headquarters and research usually located?
back: In its home country, often near universities
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why do TNCs locate manufacturing in emerging economies?
back: Lower labour costs and access to growing markets
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is vertical integration?
back: A TNC owning different stages of the same supply chain
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is horizontal integration?
back: A TNC buying or merging with firms at the same stage, often rivals
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a backward linkage for a TNC factory?
back: Local firms supplying parts or services to the factory
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is subcontracting?
back: A TNC paying another firm to make products or parts for it
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Why do TNCs use subcontractors in low-wage countries?
back: To cut costs and avoid responsibility for running factories
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is transfer pricing by a TNC?
back: Setting prices between its own branches to move profit to low-tax countries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What does it mean that a TNC is 'footloose'?
back: It is not tied to one location and can relocate easily
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is an Export Processing Zone (EPZ)?
back: An area offering tax breaks and few regulations to attract export industries
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the 'race to the bottom'?
back: Countries cutting wages, taxes or regulations to compete for TNC investment
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is the multiplier effect of a TNC factory?
back: New jobs and spending create further jobs and income locally
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is profit leakage?
back: Profits made in a host country flowing back to the TNC's home country
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: Which positive impact of TNCs comes from training local workers?
back: Transfer of skills and technology
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What negative impact can a TNC have on its home country when it moves production abroad?
back: Factory closures and job losses (deindustrialisation)
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: How do TNCs use global marketing?
back: One brand and advertising campaign promoted worldwide, adapted locally
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is a global commodity chain?
back: The linked stages a commodity goes through from producer to consumer
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: In a food commodity chain, which group usually receives the smallest share of the final price?
back: The primary producers (farmers)
point: 3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.3 International trade and access to markets

front: What is global governance?
back: The rules, norms and institutions that regulate global issues without a world government
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: In global governance, what is a norm?
back: A shared expectation of how states should behave, such as respecting human rights
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is sovereignty?
back: A state's right to govern its own territory without outside interference
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why does sovereignty limit global governance?
back: States can refuse to sign or obey international agreements
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What does it mean for a state to ratify a treaty?
back: To formally approve it, so it becomes legally binding on that state
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is an intergovernmental organisation (IGO)?
back: A body whose members are national governments, such as the UN
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is a non-governmental organisation (NGO)?
back: A non-profit body independent of government, such as Greenpeace
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What does it mean that global institutions 'reproduce' global systems?
back: Their rules keep the existing balance of power in place
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why do critics say the IMF and World Bank favour rich countries?
back: Voting power depends on money paid in, so rich countries dominate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What are IMF loan 'conditions' called?
back: Conditionality
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What were structural adjustment programmes (SAPs)?
back: IMF and World Bank loan conditions requiring spending cuts, privatisation and free trade
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why were structural adjustment programmes criticised?
back: Cuts to health and education spending hurt the poorest people
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Which economist named the 'Washington Consensus' of free-market policies in 1989?
back: John Williamson
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the main role of the IMF?
back: To keep the world financial system stable and lend to countries in crisis
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the main role of the World Bank?
back: To lend money for development projects and to reduce poverty
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the main role of the WTO?
back: To set trade rules, cut barriers and settle trade disputes between members
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the WTO's most-favoured-nation principle?
back: A trade advantage given to one member must be given to all members
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why can the WTO's dispute settlement process exacerbate inequality?
back: Poor countries lack the lawyers and money to bring cases
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why is the UN Security Council veto criticised?
back: One permanent member can block action, even on humanitarian crises
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What are UN peacekeepers?
back: Troops from member states sent with consent to keep peace after conflict
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: Why does global governance need action at the national scale?
back: National governments must pass laws to put global agreements into practice
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: How does local action link to global governance?
back: Local councils and people carry out policies, such as cutting emissions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is the free-rider problem in global governance?
back: Some states benefit from others' action without contributing themselves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is UNEP's role in global governance?
back: It coordinates UN environmental work and helps create environmental treaties
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: How can global agencies promote stability?
back: Through emergency loans, peacekeeping and agreed rules for trade
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.4 Global governance

front: What is a global common?
back: An area or resource outside any one country's control, shared by all
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Which ocean areas are global commons?
back: The high seas, beyond countries' exclusive economic zones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Which layer around the Earth is a global common?
back: The atmosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Which continent is treated as a global common?
back: Antarctica
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Beyond Earth, which area is a global common?
back: Outer space
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: How far from the coast does a country's exclusive economic zone (EEZ) extend?
back: 200 nautical miles
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Who wrote 'The Tragedy of the Commons' (1968)?
back: Garrett Hardin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What is the 'tragedy of the commons'?
back: Individuals each overuse a shared resource for their own gain, so it is destroyed
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Which economist won a Nobel Prize in 2009 for showing communities can manage commons sustainably?
back: Elinor Ostrom
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Why do global commons need global governance?
back: No single state owns them, so without rules they are overexploited
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What does the 'common heritage of mankind' principle say?
back: Resources in some commons, such as the deep seabed, belong to all humanity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What is sustainable development, as defined by the 1987 Brundtland Report?
back: Meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Why does protecting the atmosphere conflict with developing countries' right to develop?
back: Cheap fossil fuels drive growth but add to global emissions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What does 'common but differentiated responsibilities' mean in climate agreements?
back: All states must act, but richer states that polluted more should do more
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What is bioprospecting?
back: Searching wild species for genes or chemicals with commercial value
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: What does ABNJ stand for in ocean governance?
back: Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5 The 'global commons'

front: Why is Antarctica treated as a global common?
back: No state's territorial claim is recognised and it is governed jointly for peace and science
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is the Antarctic Convergence?
back: The zone where cold Antarctic surface water sinks below warmer sub-Antarctic water
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why are waters near the Antarctic Convergence so rich in life?
back: Upwelling and mixing bring nutrients and oxygen to the surface
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why is Antarctica's climate so cold?
back: High latitude, high altitude and high albedo of ice
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why is Antarctica classed as a desert?
back: It receives very little precipitation, mostly as snow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What are katabatic winds?
back: Cold, dense air flowing downhill off the ice sheet under gravity
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why are temperatures on the Antarctic coast higher than in the interior?
back: Lower altitude and the moderating effect of the sea
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is the difference between an ice shelf and sea ice?
back: An ice shelf is floating glacier ice from land, sea ice is frozen seawater
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why does melting of floating ice shelves speed up sea level rise?
back: Shelves hold back land glaciers, which then flow faster into the sea
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does loss of sea ice speed up warming in Antarctica?
back: Darker ocean absorbs more sunlight (albedo feedback)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Which tiny crustacean is the keystone species of the Southern Ocean food web?
back: Antarctic krill
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why does overfishing krill threaten the whole Southern Ocean ecosystem?
back: Whales, seals, penguins and fish all depend on krill for food
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does warming of the Southern Ocean threaten krill?
back: Less sea ice means less algae under the ice for young krill to feed on
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does ocean acidification threaten Southern Ocean species?
back: Extra dissolved CO2 makes it harder for shelled organisms to build shells
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is IUU fishing?
back: Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does longline fishing threaten Antarctic seabirds such as albatrosses?
back: Birds take baited hooks and drown
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is by-catch?
back: Animals caught unintentionally while fishing for another species
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is a maximum sustainable yield?
back: The largest catch that can be taken without reducing the stock over time
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is the 'ecosystem approach' to managing Antarctic fishing?
back: Catch limits allow for the needs of predators, not just the target species
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is the 'precautionary approach' in Antarctic management?
back: Acting to prevent harm even when scientific evidence is uncertain
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How can ships and visitors bring invasive species to Antarctica?
back: Seeds and organisms on clothing, cargo and ship hulls
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why does pollution last longer in Antarctica than in warmer places?
back: Cold temperatures slow the breakdown of waste and oil
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How can scientific research stations harm Antarctica?
back: Building, fuel spills, waste and vehicles damage fragile ground and wildlife
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does tourism threaten Antarctic wildlife?
back: Visitors disturb breeding penguin and seal colonies
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why is an oil spill from a cruise ship a serious threat in Antarctica?
back: Ice-strewn waters risk collision and oil breaks down very slowly in the cold
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why is the search for minerals a future threat to Antarctica?
back: Rising demand and better technology could make extraction profitable
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why is Antarctic governance criticised for having weak enforcement?
back: Enforcement relies on each state's own laws and decisions need consensus
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is the purpose of the International Whaling Commission (IWC)?
back: To conserve whale stocks and regulate whaling
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is a territorial claim in Antarctica?
back: A state's assertion that part of the continent belongs to it
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is an Antarctic Treaty Consultative Party?
back: A member with voting rights, usually through substantial scientific research there
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: What is an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA)?
back: A study of the likely environmental effects of an activity before it is allowed
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How do NGOs help protect Antarctica?
back: They monitor threats, campaign and lobby governments
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why do NGOs have limited power over Antarctica?
back: They cannot vote or enforce rules, only advise and campaign
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Why might NGOs be trusted more than states on Antarctic protection?
back: They are less driven by national self-interest
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: How does Antarctic governance affect people far from Antarctica?
back: Protecting its ice limits sea level rise affecting coastal people worldwide
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.5.1 Antarctica as a global common

front: Which academics (1999) grouped views on globalisation into hyperglobalists, sceptics and transformationalists?
back: David Held and colleagues (Global Transformations)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What do hyperglobalists argue about globalisation?
back: It creates a borderless world where nation-states lose power
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What do globalisation sceptics argue?
back: Globalisation is exaggerated and nation-states remain powerful
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What do transformationalists argue about globalisation?
back: It is real and reshapes states and societies, but unevenly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Which Japanese writer described a 'borderless world' (1990)?
back: Kenichi Ohmae
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Which journalist wrote 'The World Is Flat' (2005), arguing technology levels the playing field?
back: Thomas Friedman
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Which Nobel-winning economist criticised the IMF in 'Globalization and Its Discontents' (2002)?
back: Joseph Stiglitz
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Which sociologist described the spread of fast-food principles worldwide as 'McDonaldization'?
back: George Ritzer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is cultural homogenisation?
back: Cultures around the world becoming more alike, often Westernised
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: How can globalisation promote stability?
back: Trading partners are interdependent, so conflict between them is costly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is a key economic benefit of globalisation for emerging economies?
back: Rapid growth from exports and foreign investment, lifting millions out of poverty
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is a benefit of globalisation for consumers in rich countries?
back: Cheaper and wider choice of goods
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: How can globalisation increase inequality within countries?
back: Gains go mainly to skilled workers and growing cities, others are left behind
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: How can globalisation cause injustice?
back: TNCs and suppliers exploit low-paid workers with poor conditions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: How can globalisation cause conflict?
back: Competition for resources and resentment of inequality fuel tension
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: How does globalisation add to environmental damage?
back: Long-distance transport and rising consumption increase emissions and resource use
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is the pollution haven hypothesis?
back: Polluting industries move to countries with weak environmental laws
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is carbon leakage?
back: Emissions shifting to other countries when production moves out of strict ones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is reshoring?
back: Bringing production back to a company's home country
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: What is 'deglobalisation' (or 'slowbalisation')?
back: A slowdown or reversal in global integration of trade and investment
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Why does economic nationalism threaten globalisation?
back: Tariffs and trade wars reduce trade between countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: How can globalisation benefit the environment?
back: Clean technology and ideas spread faster between countries
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Which group of losers from globalisation is often linked to rising anti-globalisation politics in rich countries?
back: Workers in deindustrialised areas who lost manufacturing jobs
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.6 Globalisation critique

front: Which graph would show what share of world income goes to the poorest half of the world's population?
back: A Lorenz curve
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: What does a rising Gini coefficient for a country over time show?
back: Income inequality within the country is increasing
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Which map best shows the direction and volume of trade between trading blocs?
back: A flow line map, with line width proportional to trade
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Why should a choropleth map of trade by country use a rate such as exports per person, not totals?
back: Countries differ greatly in size and population
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Why might a logarithmic scale be used for a graph comparing exports of the USA and Malawi?
back: Their values differ by several orders of magnitude
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Which statistical test would show whether more globalised countries tend to have higher GDP per capita?
back: Spearman's rank correlation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Why does a strong correlation between KOF score and GDP per capita not prove globalisation causes wealth?
back: Wealth may drive globalisation, or a third factor may link them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Global FDI rose from US$1.45 trillion in 2023 to US$1.51 trillion in 2024 (UNCTAD). What percentage increase is this?
back: About 4%
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Why use GDP per capita rather than total GDP to compare countries' development?
back: It allows for different population sizes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: How is a country's trade balance calculated?
back: Value of exports minus value of imports
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: What is a composite index, such as the KOF Globalisation Index?
back: A single score combining several weighted indicators
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: What should you check when using NGO publicity material as qualitative evidence?
back: Its purpose and possible bias, as it is written to campaign
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Name one qualitative source for studying the impact of a TNC on workers.
back: Interviews (also: photographs, news reports, worker testimony)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Why is a single photograph limited evidence of factory working conditions?
back: It shows one moment, chosen and framed by the photographer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: Which graph best shows a TNC's sales split by world region over several years?
back: A compound (stacked) bar graph
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Global systems and global governance::3.2.1.7 Quantitative and qualitative skills

front: What is a natural hazard?
back: A natural event or process that threatens people, property or the environment

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is a disaster, as opposed to a hazard?
back: A hazard event that causes major loss of life or damage beyond a community's ability to cope

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is the term for a hazard caused by the Earth's internal processes, such as earthquakes and volcanoes?
back: Geophysical hazard
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is the term for a hazard caused by weather and climate processes, such as tropical storms?
back: Atmospheric hazard
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is the term for a hazard caused by the movement of water, such as river floods?
back: Hydrological hazard
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In hazard studies, what is vulnerability?
back: How likely people or places are to suffer harm from a hazard, and how badly
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In hazard studies, what is resilience?
back: The ability of a community to absorb, cope with and recover from a hazard event
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the disaster risk equation, risk equals hazard multiplied by vulnerability, divided by what?
back: Capacity to cope
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is the term for how people view and understand the threat posed by a hazard?
back: Hazard perception
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Why do wealthier people often perceive a hazard as less threatening than poorer people do?
back: They afford protection, insurance and recovery, so feel less exposed
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Why do some poorer people knowingly live in high-risk areas such as floodplains or volcano slopes?
back: Economic need, such as fertile land or jobs, outweighs the perceived risk
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which cultural belief leads some communities to see hazards as acts of God or fate?
back: Religious or spiritual belief (leading to fatalism)
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: How does recent personal experience of a hazard event usually affect hazard perception?
back: It raises perceived risk, so people take the threat more seriously
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: How does a long gap since the last hazard event usually affect hazard perception?
back: People become complacent and underestimate the risk
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which human response to hazards means accepting them as inevitable and doing little or nothing to reduce them?
back: Fatalism
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which human response to hazards uses scientific monitoring to forecast when and where an event will happen?
back: Prediction
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which human response to hazards means changing behaviour or the built environment to live with the hazard?
back: Adjustment (adaptation)
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which human response to hazards means actions taken to reduce the severity of a hazard's impact?
back: Mitigation
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which human response to hazards is the coordinated work of authorities before, during and after an event?
back: Management
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which human response to hazards spreads the cost of losses across many people, for example through insurance?
back: Risk sharing
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Why is fatalism more common in low-income communities?
back: People lack the money, technology and education to reduce the risk
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Why is risk sharing through insurance more common in high-income countries?
back: More people afford premiums and insurance markets are well developed
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: How does a high incidence (frequent events) of a hazard usually affect how people respond to it?
back: Frequent events encourage adaptation and preparedness as people learn to live with them
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Why do rare, very high-magnitude hazard events often overwhelm hazard management?
back: Defences and plans are designed for expected events, so extreme ones exceed them

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is a secondary impact of a hazard?
back: An effect that results from the primary impacts, such as disease or fires
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

back: Chris Park (the Park model, 1991)

subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

back: The disaster response curve
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

back: Quality of life (level of normality)

back: Time
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what is the stage when the hazard strikes and quality of life falls sharply?
back: Disruption
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what is the stage of rescue, emergency aid and medical care in the hours and days after an event?
back: Relief
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what is the stage when temporary shelter and services are restored over weeks or months?
back: Rehabilitation
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what is the final stage of rebuilding over months or years?
back: Reconstruction
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what does a curve that ends above the pre-disaster level show?
back: Quality of life improved because rebuilding was better than before
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what does a curve that ends below the pre-disaster level show?
back: The community never fully recovered, so quality of life stayed lower
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what does a very steep drop in the curve show?
back: A sudden, severe event with a rapid fall in quality of life
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the Park model, what does a long, deep trough show?
back: Slow recovery, typical of poorer places with little aid or capacity
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is one strength of the Park model for hazard managers?
back: It lets the recovery of different events be compared and planned for
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is one weakness of the Park model?
back: It is generalised and does not show different groups recovering at different rates
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Which model shows hazard management as a continuous loop of mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery?
back: The hazard management cycle
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the hazard management cycle, which stage involves planning, education and warning systems before an event?
back: Preparedness
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the hazard management cycle, which stage involves deploying emergency services to save lives during and just after an event?
back: Response
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the hazard management cycle, which stage involves rebuilding and restoring the built and natural environment?
back: Recovery
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In the hazard management cycle, which stage involves long-term steps such as building codes to reduce future impacts?
back: Mitigation
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: Why is the hazard management cycle drawn as a loop?
back: Lessons from recovery feed into mitigation and preparedness for the next event
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is one weakness of the hazard management cycle compared with the Park model?
back: It does not show timescales or how quality of life changes
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: In what way does the hazard management cycle differ from the Park model in its focus on expertise?
back: The cycle includes the role of experts and planners, which Park's model does not
point: 3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.1 The concept of hazard in a geographical context

front: What is the solid, innermost layer of the Earth, made mainly of iron and nickel?
back: The inner core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which layer of the Earth is liquid iron and nickel?
back: The outer core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the term for the rigid outer shell of the Earth, made of the crust and uppermost mantle?
back: The lithosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the term for the hot, partly molten, plastic layer of the upper mantle on which plates move?
back: The asthenosphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which type of crust is thinner, denser and made mainly of basalt?
back: Oceanic crust
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which type of crust is thicker, less dense and made mainly of granite?
back: Continental crust
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which type of crust is geologically older on average, oceanic or continental?
back: Continental crust (oceanic crust is recycled by subduction)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the main source of the Earth's internal heat?
back: Radioactive decay of elements in the mantle and core
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Apart from radioactive decay, what is the other source of the Earth's internal heat?
back: Primordial heat left over from the Earth's formation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which scientist proposed continental drift and the supercontinent Pangaea?
back: Alfred Wegener
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the name of the supercontinent that Wegener said once joined all the continents?
back: Pangaea
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which piece of evidence for continental drift is the matching coastline shapes of South America and Africa?
back: The jigsaw fit
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How do fossils support continental drift?
back: The same fossil species are found on continents now separated by oceans
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which scientist proposed sea-floor spreading in the early 1960s?
back: Harry Hess
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is sea-floor spreading?
back: New oceanic crust forms at ridges from rising magma and moves away on either side
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics
