front: What is palaeomagnetism?
back: The record of the Earth's past magnetic field preserved in cooled volcanic rock
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How does palaeomagnetism support sea-floor spreading?
back: Magnetic stripes are mirrored on either side of ocean ridges
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How does rock age change with distance from an ocean ridge?
back: Rock gets older the further it is from the ridge
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which scientist proposed that convection currents in the mantle move the plates?
back: Arthur Holmes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How do convection currents drive plate movement?
back: Hot mantle rises and spreads, then cools and sinks, dragging plates above it
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is ridge push?
back: Gravity makes new, raised lithosphere at a ridge slide away down the slope
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is slab pull?
back: The weight of a dense, sinking oceanic plate pulls the rest of the plate behind it
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which driving force is now thought to be the most important cause of plate movement?
back: Slab pull
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the term for plate movement driven by gravity as plates slide off raised ocean ridges?
back: Gravitational sliding
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is another name for a destructive plate margin?
back: A convergent margin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is another name for a constructive plate margin?
back: A divergent margin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is another name for a conservative plate margin?
back: A transform margin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: At an oceanic-continental destructive margin, why does the oceanic plate subduct?
back: It is denser than the continental plate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: At an oceanic-oceanic destructive margin, which plate subducts?
back: The older, denser plate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the term for the zone of earthquakes along a subducting plate, getting deeper inland?
back: The Benioff zone
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Why does the mantle melt above a subducting plate?
back: Water released from the slab lowers the melting point of the mantle
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Why do destructive margins produce explosive volcanoes?
back: Magma is high in silica and gas, so it is viscous and traps pressure
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which type of magma, low in silica and runny, erupts at constructive margins and hotspots?
back: Basaltic magma
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which type of magma, high in silica and viscous, erupts at destructive margins?
back: Andesitic (or rhyolitic) magma
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Why do the most powerful earthquakes occur at destructive margins?
back: Plates lock in the subduction zone, so huge stress builds before release
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Why are there no volcanoes at a conservative margin?
back: Crust is neither created nor destroyed, so no magma is produced
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What causes earthquakes at a conservative margin?
back: Plates stick as they slide past, then stress is released suddenly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Why are earthquakes at constructive margins usually shallow and fairly weak?
back: The crust is thin and stress is released as plates pull apart
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which landform forms where an oceanic plate bends down into the mantle?
back: A deep sea trench
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How do young fold mountains form?
back: Sediments between converging plates are compressed, folded and uplifted
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which type of plate margin forms fold mountains with little or no volcanic activity?
back: Continental-continental (collision) margin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How does an island arc form?
back: Magma rising above a subducting plate builds a curved line of volcanic islands
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: At which type of plate margin do island arcs form?
back: Oceanic-oceanic destructive margin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What common mistake do students make about island arcs?
back: Confusing them with hotspot island chains, which form over magma plumes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How does an ocean ridge form?
back: Magma rises where plates diverge and builds a long underwater mountain range
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Which landform forms where continental crust is pulled apart at a constructive margin?
back: A rift valley
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: How does a rift valley form?
back: Tension creates parallel faults and the block between them drops down
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the term for a block of land that drops between two parallel faults?
back: A graben
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is a magma plume?
back: A column of hot mantle rising from deep in the Earth, away from plate margins
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the surface area of volcanic activity above a magma plume called?
back: A hotspot
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Why does a magma plume produce a chain of volcanoes?
back: The plate moves over a fixed plume, so new volcanoes form as old ones move away
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: In a hotspot island chain, how does island age change with distance from the hotspot?
back: Islands get older and more eroded further from the hotspot
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What does a hotspot island chain show about the plate it sits on?
back: The direction and speed of plate movement
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the focus (hypocentre) of an earthquake?
back: The point underground where the rupture starts
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: What is the epicentre of an earthquake?
back: The point on the surface directly above the focus
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.2 Plate tectonics

front: Where do most of the world's volcanoes occur?
back: Along plate margins, especially destructive margins around the Pacific
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is the name for the belt of volcanoes and earthquakes around the Pacific Ocean?
back: The Pacific Ring of Fire
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is a pyroclastic flow?
back: A fast-moving current of hot gas, ash and rock that flows down a volcano
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is a nuée ardente?
back: A glowing cloud of superheated gas and ash, a type of pyroclastic flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why are pyroclastic flows so deadly?
back: They move very fast at hundreds of degrees Celsius, so people cannot outrun them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why do basaltic lava flows rarely kill people?
back: They usually move slowly enough for people to walk away
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is the main impact of lava flows?
back: Destruction of buildings, roads and farmland in their path
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is a lahar?
back: A volcanic mudflow of water, ash and rock that flows down river valleys
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What triggers a lahar during an eruption?
back: Rapid melting of snow and ice on the volcano
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What triggers a lahar after an eruption?
back: Heavy rain, such as from a tropical storm, washing loose ash downslope
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is tephra?
back: Any rock fragments thrown into the air by an eruption
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What size are volcanic bombs?
back: Larger than 64 mm
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What size are lapilli?
back: Between 2 mm and 64 mm
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What size is volcanic ash?
back: Smaller than 2 mm
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why does heavy ashfall cause roofs to collapse?
back: Ash is heavy, especially when wet from rain
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why is volcanic ash dangerous to aircraft?
back: It melts inside jet engines and makes them fail
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is one health impact of volcanic ash fallout?
back: Breathing problems from inhaling fine ash
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which volcanic gas reacts with water vapour to form acid rain?
back: Sulphur dioxide
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why is volcanic carbon dioxide dangerous in valleys and hollows?
back: It is denser than air, so it collects in low ground and suffocates people
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: How do large explosive eruptions cool global climate?
back: Sulphur dioxide forms aerosols in the stratosphere that reflect sunlight
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is a jökulhlaup?
back: A sudden flood caused by an eruption melting ice beneath a glacier
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What does the Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) measure?
back: The size of an eruption, from the volume of material ejected and plume height
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is the range of the Volcanic Explosivity Index?
back: 0 to 8
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: How many times more material does each step up the VEI represent?
back: About 10 times more (it is logarithmic)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which type of volcano has gentle slopes and is built from runny basaltic lava?
back: A shield volcano
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which type of volcano is steep-sided and built from layers of ash and lava?
back: A composite volcano (stratovolcano)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why are composite volcanoes at destructive margins less regular in their eruptions?
back: Long dormant periods let gas pressure build before large explosions
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is an effusive eruption?
back: A gentle eruption where runny lava flows out
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why are volcanic eruptions more predictable than earthquakes?
back: Rising magma gives warning signs such as tremors, swelling and gas release
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is a primary impact of a volcanic eruption?
back: An impact caused directly by the eruption, such as burial by a pyroclastic flow
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is a secondary impact of a volcanic eruption?
back: An impact that follows the eruption, such as lahars or famine
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is one long-term economic benefit of living near a volcano?
back: Fertile volcanic soils for farming (also: geothermal energy, tourism)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which monitoring instrument detects the small earthquakes caused by magma rising?
back: A seismometer
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is harmonic tremor?
back: Continuous ground vibration caused by magma moving, often a sign of an eruption
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which instruments detect a volcano's ground swelling as magma rises?
back: Tiltmeters (also: GPS receivers)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which satellite technique maps ground deformation on volcanoes from space?
back: InSAR (satellite radar interferometry)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What change in gas emissions warns that magma is nearing the surface?
back: An increase in sulphur dioxide released
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: How does thermal imaging help predict eruptions?
back: It detects rising ground temperature as magma approaches
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why is it impossible to prevent a volcanic eruption?
back: The forces driving magma to the surface are far too large to control
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which mitigation method uses walls, channels or water spraying to protect settlements from lava?
back: Lava diversion
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which engineering structures slow down or trap lahars in river valleys?
back: Sabo dams (also: lahar channels, dykes)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: How does building design reduce the impact of ash fallout?
back: Steep roofs that shed ash and strong roof supports
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Which preparedness method marks an area around a volcano that people must leave?
back: An exclusion zone
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: How do hazard maps help prepare for an eruption?
back: They show areas at risk from flows, so land use and evacuation are planned
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: How do volcano alert levels help preparedness?
back: They tell people and officials how close an eruption is and when to evacuate
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: Why do some people stay in danger zones despite eruption warnings?
back: Fear of losing homes, crops or livestock, or distrust of warnings
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.3 Volcanic hazards

front: What is an earthquake?
back: Ground shaking caused by the sudden release of built-up stress along a fault
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is elastic rebound theory?
back: Rocks bend as stress builds on a locked fault, then snap back when it breaks
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What depth range counts as a shallow-focus earthquake?
back: 0 to 70 km deep
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why do shallow-focus earthquakes usually cause more damage than deep ones?
back: Seismic waves lose less energy before reaching the surface
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which seismic waves are fastest and travel through both solids and liquids?
back: P waves (primary waves)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How do P waves move the ground?
back: By compression, pushing and pulling rock in the direction of travel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which seismic waves are shear waves that only travel through solids?
back: S waves (secondary waves)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which seismic waves travel along the ground surface and cause most damage?
back: Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh waves)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which surface waves shake the ground from side to side?
back: Love waves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which surface waves give a rolling motion like ocean waves?
back: Rayleigh waves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is an aftershock?
back: A smaller earthquake that follows the main shock as the crust adjusts
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which earthquake scale is now used by USGS, based on fault area, slip and rock rigidity?
back: The moment magnitude scale (Mw)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which early logarithmic earthquake scale was based on wave amplitude on a seismometer?
back: The Richter scale
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How much bigger is the wave amplitude of a magnitude 7 earthquake than a magnitude 6?
back: 10 times bigger
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Roughly how much more energy does a magnitude 7 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?
back: About 32 times more
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Roughly how much more energy does a magnitude 8 earthquake release than a magnitude 6?
back: About 1,000 times more (32 x 32)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which scale measures earthquake intensity from observed effects and damage, using Roman numerals I to XII?
back: The Modified Mercalli Intensity scale
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why does one earthquake have one magnitude but many Mercalli intensity values?
back: Intensity varies with distance, geology and building quality at each place
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How is the frequency of earthquakes related to their magnitude?
back: Low-magnitude earthquakes are far more frequent than high-magnitude ones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is meant by the randomness of earthquakes?
back: Their location along margins is known but their timing is not
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is an intraplate earthquake?
back: An earthquake far from a plate margin, often on an old fault
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is liquefaction?
back: Saturated loose sediment loses strength when shaken and behaves like a liquid
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which ground conditions are most prone to liquefaction?
back: Saturated, loose, sandy soils (such as reclaimed land and river deposits)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is one impact of liquefaction on buildings?
back: Buildings sink, tilt or collapse as the ground loses strength
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What common mistake do students make about liquefaction?
back: Treating it as a mantle process rather than a ground hazard from shaking
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How do earthquakes trigger landslides?
back: Shaking loosens material on steep slopes, which then slides downhill
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What usually causes a tsunami?
back: An undersea earthquake that suddenly lifts the seabed and displaces water
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: At which type of plate margin do most large tsunami-causing earthquakes occur?
back: Destructive (subduction) margins
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why is a tsunami hard to notice in the deep ocean?
back: Its wave height is small and its wavelength is very long
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why does a tsunami grow taller as it reaches the coast?
back: It slows in shallow water, so the wave bunches up and rises
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What natural warning sign often comes just before a tsunami reaches land?
back: The sea suddenly drawing back from the shore
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Apart from earthquakes, what else triggers tsunamis?
back: Underwater landslides (also: volcanic eruptions)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why is it not possible to predict the exact time of an earthquake?
back: There are no reliable warning signs of when a locked fault will rupture
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is seismic gap theory?
back: Parts of an active fault that have not moved for a long time are most likely to rupture next
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How does an earthquake early warning system work?
back: It detects fast P waves and warns before slower, damaging waves arrive
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How much warning does an earthquake early warning system typically give?
back: Seconds to tens of seconds
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What do DART buoys detect?
back: Changes in pressure on the deep seabed caused by passing tsunami waves
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which aseismic design feature uses rubber bearings so a building moves less than the ground?
back: Base isolation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How does cross-bracing make a building safer in an earthquake?
back: It stiffens the frame so it resists sideways shaking
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is a tuned mass damper?
back: A heavy weight at the top of a tall building that moves to counter swaying
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is retrofitting?
back: Strengthening existing buildings to resist earthquakes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why do building codes only reduce earthquake deaths if enforced?
back: Unenforced codes let unsafe buildings be built and occupied
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How does land-use zoning reduce seismic risk?
back: It keeps key buildings off land prone to liquefaction, landslides or tsunami
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: How do earthquake drills reduce deaths?
back: People learn to drop, cover and hold on instead of panicking
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Which coastal structures reduce the impact of tsunamis?
back: Sea walls (also: tsunami evacuation towers)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: Why are earthquakes in low-income countries usually more deadly than in high-income countries?
back: Poorly built housing collapses and rescue resources are limited
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.4 Seismic hazards

front: What is the minimum sea surface temperature needed for a tropical storm to form?
back: About 26.5°C (often rounded to 27°C)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: To roughly what depth must ocean water be warm for a tropical storm to form?
back: At least about 50 m
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do tropical storms not form within about 5° of the equator?
back: The Coriolis force is too weak to make the air spin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which force makes tropical storms spin?
back: The Coriolis force
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why does low vertical wind shear help tropical storms form?
back: The storm's tall structure is not torn apart by winds changing with height
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What kind of starting weather system is needed for a tropical storm to develop?
back: A pre-existing area of low pressure, such as an easterly wave
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why is high humidity in the mid-troposphere needed for a tropical storm?
back: Moist air keeps thunderstorms growing without being weakened by dry air
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What is the main energy source of a tropical storm?
back: Latent heat released when water vapour condenses
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: In tropical storm formation, what happens as warm, moist air rises over the ocean?
back: It cools and condenses, releasing latent heat that warms the air further
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why does pressure fall at the centre of a developing tropical storm?
back: Rising warm air leaves low pressure at the surface, drawing in more air
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What is the calm, clear centre of a tropical storm called?
back: The eye
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why is the eye of a tropical storm calm and cloud-free?
back: Air sinks there, warming and drying as it descends
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which part of a tropical storm has the strongest winds and heaviest rain?
back: The eye wall
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What are the spiral bands of cloud and rain outside a tropical storm's eye wall called?
back: Rainbands
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What happens to air at the top of a tropical storm?
back: It flows outwards (outflow) in the upper troposphere
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which way do tropical storms spin in the northern hemisphere?
back: Anticlockwise
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which way do tropical storms spin in the southern hemisphere?
back: Clockwise
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What are tropical storms called in the Atlantic and north-east Pacific?
back: Hurricanes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What are tropical storms called in the north-west Pacific?
back: Typhoons
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What are tropical storms called in the Indian Ocean and south Pacific?
back: Cyclones
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: At what sustained wind speed does a tropical depression become a named tropical storm?
back: 63 km/h (39 mph)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: At what sustained wind speed does a tropical storm become a hurricane?
back: 119 km/h (74 mph)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which scale classifies hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by sustained wind speed?
back: The Saffir-Simpson scale
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What sustained wind speed makes a hurricane category 5 on the Saffir-Simpson scale?
back: 252 km/h (157 mph) or more
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do tropical storms weaken when they cross land?
back: They lose their supply of warm, moist air and friction slows them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do tropical storms weaken over cold ocean water?
back: Less evaporation means less latent heat to fuel them
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Between which latitudes do most tropical storms form?
back: About 5° and 30° north and south of the equator
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: In which general direction do tropical storms move after forming?
back: Westwards, then curving away from the equator
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What is the official Atlantic hurricane season?
back: 1 June to 30 November
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What is a storm surge?
back: A rise in sea level as strong winds push water onshore and low pressure lifts the sea
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which cause of a storm surge is usually larger, wind or low pressure?
back: Strong onshore winds
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do storm surges cause the most damage at high tide?
back: The surge adds to an already high sea level, flooding further inland
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do shallow, gently sloping coasts suffer bigger storm surges?
back: Water piles up over the shallow seabed instead of spreading downwards
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do tropical storms cause river flooding far inland?
back: Very heavy rainfall over days overwhelms river channels
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why do tropical storms trigger landslides?
back: Heavy rain saturates slopes, adding weight and reducing friction
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which tropical storm hazard usually causes the most deaths?
back: Storm surge and coastal flooding
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: How do satellites help predict tropical storms?
back: They track storm formation, size and path continuously
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which aircraft fly into hurricanes to measure pressure and wind speed?
back: Hurricane hunter aircraft
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What does the cone of uncertainty on a hurricane forecast map show?
back: The likely range of the storm centre's future path
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why are false hurricane warnings a problem?
back: They cost money and make people ignore future warnings
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: How do storm shelters reduce deaths from tropical storms?
back: They give raised, strong refuges close to people's homes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: How do mangrove forests reduce tropical storm impacts?
back: They absorb wave energy and reduce storm surge reaching the coast
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: How does land-use planning reduce storm surge risk?
back: It limits building in low-lying coastal zones, keeping them for parks or beaches
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which building design feature protects homes from storm surge flooding?
back: Raising the building on stilts
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which building fixing stops hurricane winds lifting roofs off houses?
back: Hurricane straps (roof ties)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Which engineering structures protect coasts from storm surges?
back: Sea walls (also: levees, flood barriers)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: How is climate change expected to change tropical storm intensity?
back: Warmer seas give more energy, so storms become more intense with more rain
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: Why is it uncertain whether climate change will make tropical storms more frequent?
back: Records show large natural year-to-year variation in storm numbers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.5 Storm hazards

front: What is a wildfire?
back: An uncontrolled fire burning through vegetation in the countryside
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is the fire triangle?
back: The idea that a fire needs fuel, oxygen and heat
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which type of wildfire burns slowly through peat and roots below the surface?
back: A ground fire
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which type of wildfire burns leaf litter, grass and low shrubs and is the most common?
back: A surface fire
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which type of wildfire spreads through the tree canopy and is the most intense?
back: A crown fire
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What are ladder fuels?
back: Shrubs and low branches that let a surface fire climb into the tree crowns
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why do fine fuels such as dry grass and twigs ignite easily?
back: They have a large surface area and dry out quickly
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is fuel load?
back: The amount of burnable material in an area
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why does fuel continuity increase wildfire spread?
back: Unbroken fuel lets the fire move without gaps to stop it
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why is fuel moisture content important for wildfire risk?
back: Dry fuel ignites and burns much more easily than moist fuel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why do eucalyptus forests produce intense wildfires?
back: The leaves contain flammable oils and loose bark carries embers
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do some plants depend on wildfire?
back: Their seeds or cones only open or germinate after fire
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which climate type, with hot dry summers, is most prone to wildfires?
back: Mediterranean-type climates
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How does a wet spring followed by drought increase wildfire risk?
back: Rain grows lots of grass that then dries out into fuel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How does low humidity increase wildfire risk?
back: Dry air draws moisture from fuels so they ignite more easily
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do high temperatures before a fire increase wildfire risk?
back: Heat dries out vegetation and preheats fuel
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why do wildfires spread faster uphill?
back: Flames preheat and dry the fuel on the slope above
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How does wind increase wildfire spread?
back: It supplies oxygen and pushes flames and embers forward
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is spotting in a wildfire?
back: Embers carried ahead by wind start new fires beyond the fire front
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is a pyrocumulonimbus cloud?
back: A thunderstorm cloud created by a wildfire's intense heat
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is the main natural cause of wildfires?
back: Lightning (especially dry lightning)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is dry lightning?
back: Lightning from storms that produce little or no rain reaching the ground
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one deliberate human cause of wildfires?
back: Arson
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which human cause of wildfire involves utility infrastructure sparking in high winds?
back: Power lines
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which farming practice in tropical rainforests is a common cause of wildfires?
back: Slash-and-burn clearance
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one accidental human cause of wildfires?
back: Discarded cigarettes (also: campfires, sparks from machinery)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one secondary impact of a wildfire on soil?
back: Increased soil erosion and flooding because vegetation cover is lost
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one health impact of wildfire smoke?
back: Breathing problems from smoke and fine particles
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do wildfires contribute to climate change?
back: Burning vegetation releases stored carbon dioxide
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one ecological benefit of natural wildfires?
back: They clear dead material and recycle nutrients for new growth
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why have wildfire seasons become longer in many regions?
back: Climate change brings hotter, drier conditions and earlier snowmelt
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How is a fire danger rating produced?
back: By combining temperature, humidity, wind speed and fuel dryness data
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do satellites help manage wildfires?
back: They detect new fires as hot spots and track their spread
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What does the Haines Index measure for wildfire prediction?
back: Atmospheric stability and dryness linked to large fire growth
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What do live fuel moisture (greenness) maps show?
back: How green vegetation is, since greener vegetation has lower fire potential
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why is wildfire prediction useful even after a fire has started?
back: It forecasts the fire's direction and spread to plan evacuation
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do total fire bans prevent wildfires?
back: They forbid outdoor fires and risky activities on high-danger days
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do power shutoffs reduce wildfire risk?
back: Cutting power in high winds stops damaged lines sparking fires
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is controlled (prescribed) burning?
back: Deliberately burning vegetation in cool conditions to reduce fuel load
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is a firebreak?
back: A strip cleared of vegetation to stop a fire spreading
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is defensible space around a home?
back: An area cleared of flammable vegetation to slow a fire reaching the building
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How does building design reduce wildfire damage?
back: Fire-resistant materials and ember-proof vents stop houses igniting
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Which wildfire response uses aircraft to drop water or retardant on fires?
back: Aerial firefighting (water bombing)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do flame retardants help fight wildfires?
back: They coat vegetation so it does not burn easily
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one preparedness action a household takes in a fire-prone area?
back: Writing a bushfire survival plan with evacuation routes
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why is leaving early now advised as the safest wildfire response?
back: Late evacuation on smoke-filled roads is extremely dangerous
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: Why do high-income countries usually manage wildfires better?
back: They have more aircraft, trained firefighters and warning technology
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How do communities with few resources reduce wildfire risk?
back: Education, lookout spotters and local controlled burning
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: How does insurance help after a wildfire?
back: It pays for rebuilding, speeding recovery
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: What is one limitation of the hazard management cycle for wildfires?
back: Places not used to wildfires are often unprepared when unusual dry spells strike
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 1: Physical geography::Hazards::3.1.5.6 Fires in nature

front: In human geography, what is the difference between space and place?
back: Space has no meaning attached, while place is space people have given meaning to
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which geographer wrote that "what begins as undifferentiated space becomes place as we get to know it better and endow it with value"?
back: Yi-Fu Tuan (Space and Place, 1977)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In which 1977 book did Yi-Fu Tuan set out his distinction between space and place?
back: Space and Place: The Perspective of Experience
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What term did Yi-Fu Tuan use for the emotional bond or love between people and a place?
back: Topophilia
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which geographer popularised the term topophilia in a 1974 book of the same name?
back: Yi-Fu Tuan
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is the term for a fear or strong dislike of a place?
back: Topophobia
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which humanistic geographer wrote Place and Placelessness (1976)?
back: Edward Relph
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What did Edward Relph mean by placelessness?
back: Loss of distinctive local identity, so places look alike and feel alike
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which human activity did Relph blame for placelessness, through standardised buildings and mass culture?
back: Mass production and mass culture (e.g. chain stores, mass tourism)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Relph's terms, what is existential insideness?
back: The deepest belonging, where a person feels completely at home in a place without thinking about it
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Relph's terms, what is existential outsideness?
back: A deep sense of alienation, feeling a place is strange and you do not belong there
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Relph's terms, what is objective outsideness?
back: Viewing a place in a detached, scientific way, e.g. as a planner or researcher
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Relph's terms, what is vicarious insideness?
back: Feeling attached to a place experienced second-hand, e.g. through a novel, film or painting
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which geographer argued in 1987 that place has three aspects: location, locale and sense of place?
back: John Agnew
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Agnew's three aspects of place, what is location?
back: Where the place is, its fixed position on the Earth's surface (e.g. coordinates)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Agnew's three aspects of place, what is locale?
back: The physical setting for everyday life, e.g. buildings, streets and parks
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In Agnew's three aspects of place, what is sense of place?
back: The feelings and emotional attachment people have to a place
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which geographer wrote Place: A Short Introduction (2004) and defined place as a "meaningful location"?
back: Tim Cresswell
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which anthropologist coined the term non-places in a 1992 book?
back: Marc Augé
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What did Marc Augé mean by non-places?
back: Spaces of transit people pass through without forming attachment, e.g. airports, motorways
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which term did Augé link to the growth of non-places, describing an excess of time, space and individualism?
back: Supermodernity
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which geographer argued that places are open and shaped by flows, not bounded and fixed, in 'A Global Sense of Place' (1991)?
back: Doreen Massey
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is meant by Massey's progressive (global) sense of place?
back: A place's identity comes from its links to other places, not from an inward-looking past
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: According to Massey, does a place have one single, fixed identity?
back: No: places have multiple identities that keep changing
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What term did Massey use for the way different groups have unequal control over flows and movement between places?
back: Power geometry
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is meant by sense of place?
back: The subjective feelings and attachments a person has towards a place
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is meant by place identity?
back: The distinctive character of a place as people recognise it, e.g. a 'mining town'
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is an insider perspective on place?
back: The view of someone who feels at home in and belongs to a place
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is an outsider perspective on place?
back: The view of someone who feels a stranger in a place, e.g. a newcomer or tourist
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why does a long-term resident usually see a place differently from a tourist?
back: Daily lived experience gives them deeper knowledge and attachment (insider perspective)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why are insider and outsider not fixed categories for a person?
back: People move between them, e.g. a migrant becomes an insider over time
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is meant by a near place?
back: A place a person feels close to and familiar with, physically or emotionally
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is meant by a far place?
back: A place a person feels distant from and unfamiliar with, with little emotional attachment
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does a place on the other side of the world become a near place for someone?
back: Emotional ties, e.g. family links or regular visits, make it feel close
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does a place physically close to home become a far place for someone?
back: People feel no connection to it, e.g. an area they avoid or never visit
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is an experienced place?
back: A place you have lived in or visited, so you know it first-hand
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is a media place?
back: A place known only through media (e.g. TV, film, books, songs, art)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why is a media place able to become an experienced place, but not the reverse?
back: Visiting it makes it experienced, but a visit cannot be undone
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why do visitors to a media place often feel disappointed?
back: The media image was selective, so reality does not match expectations
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why do media places often give an extreme image of a place?
back: Media focus on very positive or very negative features, e.g. crime stories
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why do fictional places, such as Hogwarts, still create a sense of place?
back: Media representations give people strong feelings about them without a visit
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In the context of place, what are endogenous factors?
back: Internal factors that originate within a place and shape its character
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: In the context of place, what are exogenous factors?
back: External factors: a place's relationships and connections with other places
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is the site of a place?
back: The physical land it is built on (e.g. relief, drainage, soils, water supply)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is the situation of a place?
back: Its position relative to other places, routeways and surrounding features
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which type of factor, endogenous or exogenous, is a place's situation and accessibility to other places?
back: Exogenous (relationship with other places)
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What does topography mean?
back: The shape and form of the land surface and its features
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does valley topography affect the character of a village built along it?
back: It forms a linear village and a feeling of enclosure and isolation
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does local rock type shape the character of a place's built environment?
back: Buildings are made from local stone, giving a distinctive look
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does coastal location shape the character of a place?
back: It supports functions such as ports, fishing or seaside tourism
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does land use shape the character of a place?
back: It decides whether a place feels rural, urban, residential or industrial
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does the built environment shape the character of a place?
back: Its architecture, age and density set the visual character, e.g. Georgian terraces
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does infrastructure shape the character of a place?
back: Transport hubs such as ports, airports and railways make places busy and connected
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does an ageing population shape the character of a place?
back: It drives demand for services such as care homes and healthcare
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does ethnic diversity shape the character of a place?
back: It adds cultural features such as places of worship, food shops and festivals
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does the main employment sector shape the character of a place?
back: It shapes land use, buildings and wealth, e.g. a primary-industry or finance town
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which endogenous factor is shown by a place's age-sex structure?
back: Demographic characteristics
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Which endogenous factor is shown by a place's average income and employment types?
back: Economic characteristics
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is a clone town?
back: A town whose high street is dominated by the same chain stores as other towns
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why is a clone town an example of Relph's placelessness?
back: Chain stores make it look and feel like any other town, losing local identity
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: Why is place important in human life and experience?
back: Places give people identity, belonging, security and memories
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: What is place attachment?
back: The emotional bond a person forms with a particular place
point: 3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.1 The nature and importance of places

front: How does in-migration change the demographic characteristics of a place?
back: It changes age structure and ethnic mix, usually adding young adults
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: How does out-migration of young adults affect the age structure of a place?
back: The population ages and the birth rate falls
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: How does international migration change the cultural characteristics of a place?
back: It adds new languages, religions, foods and festivals
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is a remittance?
back: Money sent home by migrants to family in their place of origin
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is foreign direct investment (FDI)?
back: Investment by a company in business operations in another country
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is deindustrialisation?
back: The decline of manufacturing industry in a place or country
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is the main cause of deindustrialisation in the UK since the 1970s?
back: Global shift of manufacturing to lower-cost countries (globalisation)
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: Which shifting flow causes deindustrialisation in a place?
back: Investment moving away to other places, often overseas
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is disinvestment?
back: The withdrawal of investment from a place, e.g. factory closure
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is the negative multiplier effect?
back: A downward spiral where job losses cut spending, so more businesses close
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: Which economist described cumulative causation, where growth or decline in a place reinforces itself?
back: Gunnar Myrdal
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is the positive multiplier effect?
back: New investment creates jobs and spending, which creates more jobs
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is globalisation?
back: Growing interconnection of places through flows of trade, people, money and ideas
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: Which geographer used the term time-space compression in The Condition of Postmodernity (1989)?
back: David Harvey
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is time-space compression?
back: Faster transport and communications make places feel closer together
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: Who coined the term gentrification in 1964?
back: Ruth Glass
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is gentrification?
back: Wealthier people move into a poorer area, improving housing and displacing poorer residents
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Geography 7037 – Key content::Paper 2: Human geography::Changing places::3.2.2.2.1 Relationships and connections

front: What is one negative impact of gentrification on original residents?
back: Rising rents and house prices force them to move out (displacement)
